seo.title: Karmic tail 18 21 21 compatibility: a world for two
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 21 21 compatibility: The Moon at the entry and two Worlds in a row. A couple born of a shared secret builds a world for two, then must open it.

title: Karmic tail 18-21-21 in compatibility: Tristan, Iseult and a world for two
short: Karmic tail 18-21-21 in compatibility is the story of a couple born of a shared secret who build a whole world for two out of it. The Moon at the entry, The World in the middle and The World again as the main task: one card, two worlds. The first is their own, where nobody else is needed. The second is the common one, where this union still has to be brought.

sections.h2: "Not wine": The Moon at the entry
paragraphs: The legend of Tristan survives in several versions, nearly all of them incomplete: Béroul, Thomas, Eilhart, Gottfried of Strasbourg. In 1900 Joseph Bédier wove them into a single romance, and in 1913 Hilaire Belloc put it into English. Quotations below follow Belloc where he keeps the passage; where he abridges, the translation from Bédier's French is ours.

Iseult's mother brews a potion for the wedding night of her daughter and King Mark. Its power lies in one thing: "they who drink of it together love each other with their every single sense and with their every thought, forever." The pitcher is hidden, but on the ship the wind drops, the sun beats down, and a little serving maid finds it first:
And when she came on it, the child cried, "I have found you wine!" Now she had found not wine — but Passion and Joy most sharp, and Anguish without end, and Death.

Bédier opens the chapter on the potion with lines from Gottfried: "No, it was not wine, though it looked like wine" (our translation). That is The Moon. Waite calls the card "life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit"; for Wen, "Key 18 represents poetry and mystery". The Moon is a light that shows one thing in place of another. And a telling detail: the potion is drunk not at night but at midday, under a blazing sun. The Moon of this tail is not a time of day but the way two people first saw each other: a simple drink turned out to be fate.

Point M in a couple's chart, according to Lisovskaya, is what the couple strives for together: shared wishes and a "common language". The point stands on the line of tasks, so Lisovskaya also calls it the point of resistance: wishes may not fit reality. The Moon in this place is the wish for a shared secret.

In life it looks familiar. Two people were "just" colleagues for a long time, "just" pen friends, "just" friends of friends, and never noticed when "just" ended. Or the first months of the union were spent in secret — from parents, from a shared circle of friends, from past relationships: "let's not tell anyone yet." From the first day such a couple has something only the two of them know about, and it binds them more tightly than any vow.

sections.h2: Chips in the stream: a language that needs no words
paragraphs: Tristan is banished from the castle, and Brangien teaches him a ruse. Behind Tintagel there is an orchard, in the orchard a pine, under the pine a spring, and its water runs straight through the women's rooms:

And every evening, by Brangien's counsel, Tristan cut him twigs and bark, leapt the sharp stakes and, having come beneath the pine, threw them into the clear spring; they floated light as foam down the stream to the women's rooms; and Iseult watched for their coming.

This is how The Moon speaks: in signs, not words. In Marie de France's lai "Chevrefoil" (The Honeysuckle), Tristan carves his name on a hazel rod with honeysuckle wound around it and lays it on the queen's road. Part the hazel and the honeysuckle, and both wither. Marie sums up the message in one line: "Sweet love, so it is with us: neither you without me, nor I without you" (our translation). In Wagner the agreed sign is different: Isolde herself puts out the torch.
The great scene of this language is the night under the pine. Warned by a dwarf, the King hides in the branches:

That night the moon shone clear. Hid in the branches the King saw his nephew leap the pallisades and throw his bark and twigs into the stream. But Tristan had bent over the round well to throw them and so doing had seen the image of the King. He could not stop the branches as they floated away.

Iseult sees the reflection too and does not raise her eyes. For the hidden listener the two act out a scene of innocence, and the King in the branches smiles. The moonlight has saved them: they know how to read reflections. But from that night their love has to be performed. And a sign has a property a word lacks: it cannot be recalled. The chips are already floating towards Iseult, and Tristan cannot stop them.

For a couple with The Moon at the entry this is a gift: understanding each other by a glance across the room, by a pause in a conversation, by a song sent instead of a letter. It is also a trap. A sign always has to be deciphered, and the guess is not always right. "I sent you that song — you were supposed to get it." "I was silent all evening — wasn't it obvious?" Silence is read as cooling, tiredness as hurt. Among The Moon's tasks Lisovskaya lists what grows out of this language: hiding feelings and treating tenderness as weakness, jealousy over invented stories. For Wen the reversed Moon carries "risk of misunderstandings in the relationship".

sections.h2: The orchard behind a wall of air: what The Moon really wants
paragraphs: On one of those nights under the pine, before the King ever climbed into the branches, Iseult says a sentence that holds the whole tail:

Is this not the wonderful orchard the harp lays tell of? A wall of air encloses it on every side; the trees are in flower, the ground is fragrant; the knight lives there without growing old in the arms of his love, and no hostile power can break the wall of air…

"No," said Tristan, "the wall of air is broken already, and this is not the wonderful orchard. But one day, my love, we shall go together to the happy land from which no one returns. <…> The sun does not shine there, and yet no one misses its light."

Here is the knot of 18-21-21. The Moon at the entry does not want secrecy for its own sake — it wants a World. An orchard walled in by air is a whole world where nothing grows old and nobody interferes. Only this world has a condition: there is no sun in it. The world the couple sees at the entry is a world without daylight.

This is the resistance of point M. Tristan already knows the wall is broken, and still he promises a land without sun. Every such couple recognises its own wall of air: "we're not like everyone else", "nobody understands us, and that's fine". It is true, and it is beautiful. But on the towers of Tintagel the trumpets are already sounding the dawn.

sections.h2: The wood of Morois: a middle where the whole world is two people
paragraphs: The secret comes out, and the King condemns them both to the stake without a trial. Tristan leaps from a chapel on the cliffs, snatches Iseult from the lepers she has been handed to, and the two go into the wood of Morois. The middle of the tail is The World, and in Waite's divinatory list The World has "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". In the forest this is literal:

They wandered in the depths of the wild wood, restless and in haste like beasts that are hunted, nor did they often dare to return by night to the shelter of yesterday. <…> They loved each other and they did not know that they suffered.

Bédier opens the chapter on the forest with a dialogue from the thirteenth-century prose Tristan: "We have lost the world, and the world has lost us. What do you say to that, Tristan, my friend? — My love, when I have you with me, what do I lack? If the whole world were with us now, I would see no one but you" (our translation). The whole world is squeezed into one person. That is The World in the place of the middle: the couple walks the road as an entire universe of two.

Gottfried of Strasbourg goes further and gives this universe an address — the lovers' cave, la fossiure a la gent amant (here and below, Gottfried in our translation from Middle High German). The cave is "round, wide, high and upright, snow-white, smooth all round", and in the middle stands a bed of crystal. What did the two live on? "They looked at each other, and that was their food." And more:
And what need had they of anyone else in there? They had an even company — one and one more. Add anyone to the two of them, and it would have become odd.

"Whatever anyone anywhere in the world could call the life they wished for, they had it all there." This is The World at its best, and it is real. Lisovskaya writes of such a couple: a shared philosophy of life on which the two came together; many roads and moves; for many people, an ideal couple. Gottfried reads the round shape of the cave like this: the roundness inside is the simplicity of love, love should have no corners, and "the corner in love is malice and cunning". In the forest there is nobody to hide from, and The Moon's ruses are no longer needed: two people who spoke in signs for years live without tricks for the first time.

In life this is the season such couples remember as their best. A move to another city where nobody knows them. A long road for two. Their own rituals, their own vocabulary, weekends to which nobody is invited. "We're fine on our own" — and it is true.

But The World also has Waite's reversed list: "inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence". In the forest both lists come true at once: every night the two change their shelter, and nothing changes. It is flight on the spot. Even the floor of Gottfried's cave is green marble, and it stands for constancy. For Gottfried that is a virtue of love, but marble also does not move. Lisovskaya calls The World at its worst a Groundhog Day. And the hound Husdent, who found his master in the forest, is trained by Tristan within a month to hunt in silence. In a world for two even the dog may not give voice.

sections.h2: Two Worlds in a row: why the middle equals the task
paragraphs: In a personal chart the middle of the tail is the reduced sum of the two outer numbers. If a couple had that formula, the middle would come out as 18 + 21 = 39 → 12, The Hanged Man. But a couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles: 16 + 5, 12 + 9 or 8 + 13. The result is 21, and in a personal chart such a middle with such outer numbers does not occur. The World in the middle is a card the two create only together.

A repeated arcanum does not mean there is "twice as much" World. These are two roles. The same line from the prose romance tells them apart best: "We have lost the world, and the world has lost us." The middle is the world the couple has: the forest, the cave, the island. The main task is the world it has lost: the court, friends, family, the day. Gottfried, having described a cave where the two had everything, leaves a single crack: for a better life they would not have given a bean — "except only for their honour". Honour is the second world, the eyes of other people.

The trap of this tail is to take the middle for the end: "we've built our own world, the task is done." The main task of a tail is read mostly through its negative side, and The World at its worst, in Lisovskaya, is exactly what a cave without an exit turns into. There are no agreements, and each pulls the blanket their way. The partner's interests meet harsh criticism. Seeing friends and family is forbidden, the partner is shut inside four walls. The relationship cannot end, and the two keep coming together and breaking apart. Wen sees in the reversed World someone "afraid of change" and "consciously and knowingly in denial".

At its best the same card says the opposite. Wen calls The World "the card of synthesis" and writes that to fulfil one's purpose one "must embrace the spiritual dimension" of one's "relationship with his or her environment". For a couple this is the task: not to choose between their own world and the common one, but to stitch them together.

There is also a quiet hint in the arithmetic. Lisovskaya allows repeated energies to be added: 21 + 21 = 42 → 6. Two Worlds give The Lovers, and so does the whole tail: 18 + 21 + 21 = 60 → 6. The card of choice does not stand in the tail, yet it comes out as its sum. The potion took choice away from the two; the tail gives it back as a total. By Lisovskaya's rule such a sum, if it does not appear in the chart, sounds faintly, as a "trail". In 6.2% of these couples The Lovers stands in the centre, and then the hint sounds at full voice.

sections.h2: A sword between the sleepers: the world knocks at the door
paragraphs: The most important scene for the main task happens on a summer day in the forest. Tristan comes back from hunting, both fall asleep in their hut, fully clothed, with a naked sword lying between them. A forester gives them away, the King comes alone with a drawn sword, already raises it — and sees the sword between the sleepers. There will be no blow. And then:

The sun, passing through the hut, burned Iseult's white face. The King took his gloves trimmed with ermine. "It was she," he remembered, "who brought them to me from Ireland." He set them in the leaves to stop the hole through which the ray came down…
Mark exchanges the rings and the swords and leaves. The world the two had hidden from for years has come to them and shaded the sleeping woman's face from the sun. What do the two see when they wake?
"Yes," said Tristan, "he has carried off my sword; he was alone, he took fright and went for reinforcements. He will come back and have us burned before all the people. Let us flee!"

And they flee — towards the border of Wales, deeper into the forest. A gesture of mercy is read as a threat. Three days later, at night, Tristan understands: "It was not fear that moved the King… It was not pardon it was understanding." Meanwhile, in the thicket, "the golden ring that King Mark had slipped there glistened on her finger in the moonlight", and Iseult reads it anew: it was given not by the angry man who handed her to the lepers but by the lord who once took her in. The light is the same, moonlight, but the reading is different.

This is the great fork of 18-21-21. The Moon at the entry can read the world's signs through fear, or through the truth. To a couple used to secrecy, any gesture from outside looks like an intrusion. A partner's mother brings food: "she's checking up on us." Friends invite them to a party: "they want to split us up." A colleague helps out: "what does he want from you?" The couple "flees to Wales": fewer people, thicker walls. The first skill of the main task is checking the reading. What is in the leaves: a threat, or a glove?

sections.h2: A potion for three years: the fourth card neither of them has
paragraphs: Why can't the two simply walk out of the forest? The answer stands in the centre of the chart. A couple's centre is the shared atmosphere of the union, what lies between the two and is not on show. In 93.8% of couples with this tail The Devil stands there, and no birth date at all has The Devil in the centre of a personal chart. This card is the potion exactly: neither has it alone, and it works only on those who "drink of it together". Brangien names the culprit outright: "that old Enemy has tricked us, all us three". On the third day, as evening falls, the two on the ship are already "bound for ever".

In Lisovskaya, The Devil in a couple's atmosphere means, at its best, passion, powerful support, the ability to accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes. At its worst: the wish to own the partner, jealousy, and a union held together by intimacy alone. To the hermit Ogrin, Tristan speaks the language of that worst side: "henceforth she is altogether mine. She cannot pass from me nor I from her." Lisovskaya's chapter on The Devil ends with the opposite thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

And here the authors of the legend have been arguing for eight hundred years. In Gottfried and Thomas the potion has no term: Gottfried calls it "the endless anguish of the heart, of which both died", and Thomas's line in Bédier's epigraph reads "in the drink was our death". But in Béroul, Iseult's mother brewed it "for three years of love" (all three in our translation). On the day after St John's Day the three years run out, and Tristan, in the middle of a hunt, suddenly sees his life from outside: "I have forgotten chivalry, the court and the barons." He feels sorry for the queen to whom he gives "a hut instead of bed-curtains". Love has not ended. The spell has, and choice has come back.

A couple with The Devil in the centre may also have a spell from day one: "we couldn't be without each other", "it was like an electric shock". The question is not whether there is a potion but which version to read it by — Thomas's or Béroul's. A chain for ever, or the first years of enchantment, after which there remain two people able to choose.

sections.h2: Waite on The Moon, The World and The Devil: reflected light and a chain of flowers
paragraphs: Waite describes the designs of his cards, and three of those descriptions fit the legend almost without a gap.

The path between the towers of The Moon he calls "the issue into the unknown", and the dog and the wolf "the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit, when there is only reflected light to guide it". That is the waking in the hut: fear comes precisely at the exit, at the moment when the world itself holds out a hand.

The World's wreath in Waite is "an elliptic garland, as if it were a chain of flowers". He reports Éliphas Lévi's view that such a chain is "less easily broken than a chain of iron". In Bédier's romance this chain runs from the first chapter to the last. After the potion it seems to Tristan "as though an ardent briar, sharp-thorned but with flower most sweet smelling, drave roots into his blood". And in the last chapter there springs from Tristan's tomb "a green and leafy briar, strong in its branches and in the scent of its flowers", which reaches into Iseult's tomb. "Thrice did the peasants cut it down, but thrice it grew again", and the King forbids them to touch it. Bédier begins and ends his romance with the same plant: The World's chain of flowers.

Above the two figures of The Devil, Waite places a being of whom he says that he "is not to be their master for ever". The Devil's divinatory list contains "fatality" — and, at once, a proviso: "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". This is Béroul's version written in the language of the Tarot: the potion is fated, but not for ever and not for evil.

sections.h2: The hermit's letter and the Ford: a way out written into the legend
paragraphs: The couple's values are its shared road and what keeps the union afloat. In 63.8% of couples with tail 18-21-21 The Hermit stands there. The legend has its own hermit, Brother Ogrin, and his role is unexpected: a man of solitude leads two people out of their solitude. Gottfried even calls the cave a clûse, the word for a hermit's cell.

In Béroul this happens when the three years run out; in Bédier, after the night when both understood what the King's gloves meant. The two come to Ogrin. Tristan asks for help to offer the King peace, and the hermit "took ink, and wrote a little writ offering the King what Tristan said". These are the first plain words in which their love addresses the world: not chips, not a rod with a name, not a reflection in water, but a letter. The Moon still holds on: Tristan carries the letter by night and lays it on the window grille, and when the King cries three times into the dark, "Tristan! Tristan! Tristan, my son!", Tristan is already far away. But the word has been spoken.

Then comes a scene worth remembering for every couple with this tail. The old man "hobbled upon his crutch to the place called The Mount" and spends everything he has saved for years on furs, silk, "a shift whiter than the lily" and a palfrey harnessed in gold, "and the folk laughed to see him spending upon these the small moneys he had amassed so long". The hermit's explanation is simple:

"Queen, your clothes are falling to rags. Accept these gifts, so that you may be more beautiful on the day you go to the Ford. I only fear they will not please you: I am no expert at choosing a woman's finery."

The Ford is the place where two worlds meet. The King announces that there "he would make his peace with the Queen", and on the appointed day the people come out to meet her; "the gates of the palace were thrown open that rich and poor might enter and eat and drink at will". This is The World at its best — a world restored for everyone, not just for two.

Gottfried also has an image of how this is possible without tearing down the cave. The cave's door is of bronze, with neither lock nor key on the outside: whoever goes in at love's door when nobody lets them in from inside — that is "not love, but falsehood or force". And under the vault three windows are cut: kindness, humility and courtesy. Through them shines in "honour, the best of all lights". The cave does not have to be pulled down — it needs windows.

The legend is honest about something else too. "But Tristan that night hid with Orri, as the Queen had counselled him" — in a ruined cellar at the forester's. The secret returned a few hours after the peace. This is where the "together, apart, together again" of The World's worst side begins. The main task is not a single return but the habit of returning to the Ford.

In the remaining 36.2% of couples The Moon stands among the values — the same card as at the entry. Then the secret of the union itself is not a flaw to be fixed but a value to be kept. The couple is right to keep its cave. The task is to cut windows, not walls.

sections.h2: The shadow of the tail: a crystal chamber and a black sail
paragraphs: The legend takes the worst of this tail all the way to the end as well. Later Tristan comes back to Mark disguised as a fool, and the King asks in jest where he would take the queen:

"Up there, between the sky and the clouds, in my fair house of glass. The sun passes through it with its rays, the winds cannot shake it; I will carry the queen there, into a chamber of crystal all in flower with roses, all shining in the morning when the sun strikes it."

A world for two that exists only in the air. Then comes the scene of recognition. Iseult does not recognise Tristan; the hound Husdent knows him at once. She gives in only when she sees the ring of green jasper, their agreed sign. And she explains: "we are wrapped in ruses <…>. Neither your reminders of our past life, nor the sound of your voice, nor this very ring proves anything to me, for all of it may be the wicked work of an enchanter." Tristan answers: "What does the ring matter? <…> It was the sound of my heart you should have heard!"

This is the limit of The Moon's language: there are so many signs that even a lover needs a password. In Wagner the shadow of the tail sounds at full volume. Night is the realm of love, day is the enemy, and in the second act the two beg the night: "löse von der Welt mich los!" — "release me from the world!" Isolde's last words in the opera are to drown "in des Welt-Atems wehendem All", in the wafting universe of the world's breath (our translation). The world is swallowed by night. And in Wagner's last act King Marke sails in to unite the two — too late.

In Bédier the end is decided by a last sign. The dying Tristan makes an arrangement with a friend: "if you bring Iseult, hoist the white sail; but if you bring her not, the black." The sail comes in white, but it is not Tristan who looks at it; it is Iseult of the White Hands: "For its colour, why, it is black." A couple whose language was signs perishes by a sign that someone else read for them.

This is not a prediction. The legend is the version in which The Moon won every time. The tail of a living couple promises neither tragedy nor happiness; it shows where the fork lies. One more thing deserves saying about what the tail does not contain. If a world for two turns into bans on seeing friends, into surveillance and threats, that is not a "karmic task" but a reason to talk to a couples counsellor, and in danger to call a local emergency number.
The legend itself suggests what works. All of these are actions, not moods:

ul: **Turn the sign into a word.** Ogrin wrote down in words what the two had been saying with wood chips for years. The song, the pause, the look stay, but the main thing is said aloud at least once.
**Check the reading.** Before "fleeing to Wales", ask: is it a threat in the leaves, or a glove? A gesture from family, friends or colleagues is first clarified, then interpreted.
**Keep three windows.** Kindness, humility and courtesy towards those outside. Through them honour enters the cave — the way people see the couple.
**Find a Ford.** A place where the couple is seen as a couple: a shared celebration, guests, people who know them both.
**Don't mistake the middle for the end.** A world of their own is a road, not a destination. The main task begins where the world for two is ready.
**Let the dog bark.** Each has a voice of their own, friends of their own and pursuits beyond "our world", and that is no betrayal of the union.

paragraphs: The strong version of tail 18-21-21 is a couple who have a secret of their own and who bring it into the world instead of hiding it from the world. Having described the cave, Gottfried suddenly confesses: "This I know well, for I was there." And he adds: "I have known the cave since I was eleven, and I never came to Cornwall." The cave is not a place in a forest but something two people carry with them. It does not need to be guarded with walls. It can be carried to the Ford, to a celebration, into a city full of people — and it will still be the cave.

sections.h2: How to find tail 18-21-21 from two birth dates
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's chart is the sum of the same points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. Example: the dates 10.01.1977 and 14.04.1975.

For the first date the day is 10, the month 1, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 7 = 24 → 6. The karmic task D = 10 + 1 + 6 = 17, the centre 10 + 1 + 6 + 17 = 34 → 7, the entry M = 17 + 7 = 24 → 6, the middle N = 17 + 6 = 23 → 5. The personal tail is 6-5-17.

For the second date the day is 14, the month 4, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. D = 14 + 4 + 22 = 40 → 4, the centre 14 + 4 + 22 + 4 = 44 → 8, M = 4 + 8 = 12, N = 4 + 12 = 16. The personal tail is 12-16-4.
The couple's tail: entry 6 + 12 = 18, middle 5 + 16 = 21, task 17 + 4 = 21. The couple's centre is 7 + 8 = 15, The Devil; the couple's values are The Hermit.
What else shows across all dates from 1900 to 2026:

ul: **Rarity.** Tail 18-21-21 occurs in roughly one couple in 230 (0.435%), 61st place among the 97 couple tails. There are no other couple tails made of these three numbers.
**Couples only.** As a personal tail 18-21-21 never occurs: in a personal chart the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a task of 21 an entry of 18 cannot come out with any centre.

**What it is made of.** Three combinations of personal tails: 12-16-4 + 6-5-17 (55% of such couples), 9-12-3 + 9-9-18 (39%), 15-8-11 + 3-13-10 (6%). Neither partner brings The Moon to the entry: it comes out of 12 + 6, 9 + 9 or 15 + 3.

**Centre.** The Devil in 93.8% of couples, The Lovers in 6.2%. Curiously, The Lovers stands in the centre precisely for the combination 15-8-11 + 3-13-10, where The Devil is already present in the personal tail of one of the two.
**The couple's values.** The Hermit in 63.8%, The Moon in 36.2%.

intro: This triple has two oddities, and both can be seen without any mysticism. The middle and the main task are the same card: the couple's road and its goal coincide, and it is easy to decide the task is already done. And in the centre of 93.8% of these couples stands The Devil, a card that never appears in the centre of a personal chart. It comes into being only when two people add up to a couple.

ul: **M · The Moon — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a secret of its own and a language of its own, something only the two of them understand. Here too lies the resistance: a life by moonlight does not sit easily with the day.
**N · The World — middle of the task.** How the couple walks the road: out of the secret grows a whole world for two — a home, a road, an island where nobody else is needed.

**D · The World — main task.** What there is to learn: to bring this world out to people. At its worst it means walls, isolation and "together, apart, together again". At its best, agreements spoken in words and a world with room for the couple and for everyone else.

intro: This story was written down eight hundred years ago, and everyone knows it: Tristan and Iseult. A potion drunk by two by mistake. Wood chips sent down a stream instead of letters. A forest where two people live as a whole world. A king who finds them asleep and shields Iseult's face from the sun. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the three cards, in the books and in the numbers of this tail.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 18-21-21 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the story of a couple that begins with a shared secret (The Moon at the entry), walks its road as a whole world for two (The World in the middle) and learns to bring that world out to people (The World as the main task). The main risk is walls around the union; the main strength is a world of their own that is not afraid of daylight.

faq.q: Why does the couple's tail have two Worlds in a row?
faq.a: A couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles, not from the outer numbers, so it can coincide with the task. The two World cards are two roles: in the middle it is the world the couple has, in the task it is the common world it still has to win back.

No. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre, and with a task of 21 an entry of 18 cannot come out with any centre. This triple arises only in a couple's chart, from the sum of two personal tails.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: A couple's tail is never good or bad: it shows a task, not a verdict. The strength of 18-21-21 is depth and a universe of its own; its weakness is isolation. Which wins is up to the two: in the legend this story has both the black sail and the Ford.

faq.q: What stands in the centre for couples with tail 18-21-21?
faq.a: In 93.8% of these couples The Devil stands in the centre — an atmosphere of passion and a strong bond that never appears in the centre of a personal chart. In 6.2% it is The Lovers. The couple's values are The Hermit or The Moon.

The Moon at the entry, The World in the middle and The World again as the main task. One card, two worlds: their own, where nobody else is needed, and the common one, where this union still has to be brought.

In the legend the potion works only on those who drink it together. In the centre of these couples there is almost always The Devil, a card that never appears in the centre of a personal chart. It comes into being only when two people add up to a couple. Brangien, who guarded the pitcher, says as much: "that old Enemy has tricked us, all us three".

report.h3: The Moon speaks in wood chips, not words

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its common language. The Moon's language is signs. Every evening the banished Tristan throws bits of bark into a spring, the stream carries them through the women's rooms, and Iseult knows it is time. One night the moon lights up the water, and both see in it the reflection of the King, hidden in the branches of the pine. The two act out a scene of innocence for him and are saved. They know how to read reflections. But from that night their love has to be performed.

For a couple with 18-21-21 this is a gift: understanding each other by a glance across the room, by a pause, by a song sent instead of a letter. It is also a trap. A sign has to be deciphered, and the guess is not always right. Silence is read as cooling, tiredness as hurt, and a sign cannot be taken back: the chips are already floating.

What such a Moon wants, Iseult says plainly. She dreams of a wonderful orchard enclosed on every side by a wall of air, where nobody grows old and no hostile power can break the wall. Tristan promises her "the happy land from which no one returns": "The sun does not shine there, and yet no one misses its light." **The Moon at the entry wants a whole World — but a world without daylight.**

report.h3: A cave that has everything but one thing

report: The middle of the tail is The World, and in the legend it is the wood of Morois, where the two flee from the stake. In Gottfried of Strasbourg the forest has a heart: the round cave of lovers with its bed of crystal. "And what need had they of anyone else in there? They had an even company — one and one more. Add anyone to the two of them, and it would have become odd."

This is a real strength: a couple that walks its road as an entire universe of two. Moves, roads, rituals of their own, weekends to which nobody is invited. In the cave there is not even any need for ruses, since there is nobody to hide from. But Gottfried leaves a single crack: for a better life the two would not have given a bean — "except only for their honour". Honour is the second world, the eyes of other people.

**The trap of this tail is to take the middle for the end.** The main task is the same World card, and at its worst it looks like a cave without an exit: friends and family cut off, the partner's interests under suspicion, the two coming together and breaking apart, each day like the one before.

The most important scene for the main task happens in the forest. The King finds the two asleep, a naked sword between them. There will be no blow. A ray of sun falls on Iseult's face, and the King stops the gap in the leaves with his gloves. He exchanges the rings and the swords and leaves. The two wake, and Tristan says: "he was alone, he took fright and went for reinforcements. <…> Let us flee!" They run deeper into the forest.

**A gesture of mercy is read as a threat.** To a couple used to secrecy, any gesture from outside looks like an intrusion: a partner's mother brings food — "she's checking up on us"; friends invite them to a party — "they want to split us up". Three days later Tristan understands: "It was not pardon it was understanding." The first skill of the main task is checking the reading: what is in the leaves, a threat or a glove?

report.h3: The hermit's letter and three windows

report: The legend writes the way out in just as much detail. The hermit Ogrin writes a letter to the King on behalf of the two: the first plain words in which their love addresses the world, not wood chips and not a reflection in water. Then the old man on his crutch spends everything he has saved for years on silk and furs, so that the queen may be more beautiful on the day she goes to the Ford. At the Ford the King makes his peace with the queen, and the gates of the palace stand open to all.

Gottfried has an image of how to keep the cave without locking oneself inside. Under its vault three windows are cut — kindness, humility and courtesy — and through them shines in "honour, the best of all lights". **The cave does not have to be pulled down — it needs windows.**

The legend is honest about something else as well: that same night after the Ford, Tristan secretly hides in a forester's cellar. So the task is not a single return but the habit of returning. Otherwise the Moon's language reaches its limit: even a lover needs a password, and the last sign — a white sail or a black one — is read for the two by someone else. If a world for two turns into bans on seeing friends, into surveillance and threats, that is not a karmic task but a reason to talk to a couples counsellor, and in danger to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

The strong version of the tail is a couple who have a secret of their own and bring it into the world instead of hiding it from the world. Gottfried confesses: "I have known the cave since I was eleven, and I never came to Cornwall." The cave is not a place in a forest but something two people carry with them.

unit.meaning: Your task is to bring your world for two out to people: speak in words, not signs, and cut windows in the cave.
